newsitem.title: USA: Stock prices extend recovery into second day.
newsitem.headline: Stock prices extend recovery into second day.

text.p: Stock prices rose again Tuesday, extending their recovery from Friday's sell-off that was sparked by cautionary comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.
Gains in technology stocks lent strength to the rally, sending the Nasdaq index further into record territory.
At 1 p.m. EST, the Dow Jones industrial average was up 27.95 points at 6,491.89 after jumping 82 points Monday.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 13-10 on active volume of 251 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

"It seems the market is buoyed by strength in technology stocks. And at current levels Greenspan appears to be a lonely bear. No rate hike is seen soon," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co.

Greenspan sent stocks into a tailspin Friday with a warning about "irrational exuberance" in financial markets. The comments sparked a sell-off of 145 points in the Dow before it recovered to end the day with a loss of 55 points.
The technology-studded Nasdaq Composite index pushed further into record ground, gaining 7.35 points at 1,323.62 to surpass Monday's record of 1,316.27.
The American Stock Exchange index was up 1.39 at 591.87.
The technology sector was propelled by news that the November book-to-bill ratio, a gauge of the semi-conductor industry's activity, rose to 1.15 from an upwardly revised 1.11 in October.
A flat to slightly higher reading had been expected. The ratio means that manufacturers received $115 in new orders last month for every $100 in shipments.

Among tech stocks, chip heavyweight Intel rose 2-1/8 to 132-1/4 after hitting a 52-week high of 133-3/8. Motorola rose 7/8 to 55-7/8, International Business Machines was up 1/2 to 160-1/2, Microsoft rose 2-1/8 to 83-7/8 and Dell Computer added 2-1/2 to 63.
Joseph Battipaglia, chief investment officer at Gruntal & Co., said big-name technology companies such as Microsoft and Intel have "had big jumps and Nasdaq can go higher."
But he said he believed the "story of 1997" will be a transition to smaller stocks from big-name companies.
Wall Street still faces several key economic indicators this week, including the Producer Price Index for November, which is due Wednesday and Consumer Price Index and retail sales on Thursday.

Among special situations, Black & Decker slumped 6-1/8 to 31-1/2 after forecasting its fourth-quarter and 1996 results would fall below expectations. It also warned that its 1997 first-quarter earnings will fall below year-ago levels.
"The market continues to penalise stocks with bad news. Black & Decker is no exception," Ackerman said.
Philip Morris rose 2-1/4 to 116-1/2, with analysts citing continued buying momentum after Goldman Sachs on Monday raised its 12-month price target for the stock to $135 from $125.
Komag slumped 5-5/16 to 27-13/16 after warning that its fourth-quarter results would fall below expectations.

Bay Networks lost 2 to 22-5/8. Bay's new chief executive officer said the company's earnings will be flat or near flat until Bay tackled issues that included ineffective marketing and a lack of focus.
